claims.assertion: This is a metered RydeTAXI trip (F8 total $61.32 with a distance component of $43.64 over 30.95 km), so diversion km feed straight into the fare and the RD-2 mileage refund applies.

The rider's consent is the single message “Sure, your call.” at 18:43 (F10), sent in reply to the driver's 18:42 question “ok if I go round via Rifle Range Road?” (F9); it is a passenger message sent before the first segment started at 18:46, so it satisfies the timing requirement of RD-5 for that segment only.

The rider's “Sure, your call.” is at most a general route authorisation, not a named-road authorisation: the only named road in the chat is Rifle Range Road (F9), and no fact ties the 18:46–18:56 segment (F3) to Rifle Range Road — the segment merely runs up to 1923 m away from the optimal route (F3). The judge may therefore find its scope undetermined.

Even if consent covers the first deviation, the second segment (19:03–19:12, +4.78 km, up to 1680 m off route, F4) lies outside it: the consent message is timestamped 18:43 (F10), before that segment started at 19:03, and there is no rider message authorising any route change after 18:43 (F9–F11).

The driver's post-trip statement that “the second turn-off was my GPS rerouting” (F12) is a statement, not consent (G11), and after-the-fact notification is not agreement “before you go”; it loses to the GPS and chat system records (F4, F10).

No traffic exemption is available for the second segment: the only congestion records are speed band 4 (30–39 km/h) on BKE and PIE (F13, F14), which is neither band 1 nor band 2, and there are no incidents at all near the route (F15) — RD-4(a) is unmet and RD-4(b) band evidence is absent.

The second segment is therefore an unexempted off-route segment and the refund is 4.78 km × the trip's per-km rate $1.4100 (F5, computed as fare distance fare ÷ distance km) = $6.74, rounded to the cent, with the excess-distance line billed at $14.64 for 10.38 km (F5) confirming the rate.
The waiting line of $0.11 (F6) is a RydeTAXI meter waiting unit and is not refundable under RD-3(c), and the platform fee $1.47 is a published Ryde charge (F8), so neither is disputed.

The driver's 90-day record shows 3 disputes with 1 upheld, though none of those upheld is a route dispute (F18); because no route dispute against this driver is recorded as upheld, the RD-6 precondition of route_disputes_upheld_90d ≥ 1 is not evidenced on this file, so we do not press for flag_account.

weaknesses: The rider did send an authorising message before the first deviation: “Sure, your call.” at 18:43 (F10) replying to the driver's 18:42 proposal to go round via Rifle Range Road (F9). The driver will argue this general discretion covers both deviations, which would defeat part or all of the claim if the judge reads “your call” as covering the whole trip's routing; our answer is only that the second segment (F4) began at 19:03, twenty minutes after the last rider message, and that 'your call' cannot stretch to a later, separate deviation.

For the first segment the driver's position is stronger than ours: there is a named road (Rifle Range Road, F9) and a pre-segment consent (F10), and if the judge infers the 18:46–18:56 segment (F3) was on that road the segment is exempt; we cannot cite any fact tying the driven path to the road name, so that segment is at best undetermined (G13) and not refundable on this record.

There is no % / km threshold in the policy (RD-1), so the driver can characterise a 4.78 km, 1680 m-away loop (F4) as minor map-matching or 'GPS re-routing' noise; we must rely on it being a full separate off-route segment recognised by the fact tool.
